messages.content: I want to develop tactile slip prediction that distinguishes impending grasp slip from elastic deformation, even across unseen materials and sensor wear. The prediction must come at least 100 milliseconds before slip, with at least 90% recall and no more than a 5% false-positive rate. Those targets also have to hold on held-out materials and worn sensors, including deformation-only contacts matched for force.

The goal is to anticipate grasp slip rather than merely recognize it once it is happening, while avoiding alarms when a contact deforms elastically without slipping. The timing and error targets are joint requirements: a useful prediction must be at least 100 milliseconds early, reach ≥90% recall, and keep the false-positive rate at ≤5%. Performance on held-out materials and worn sensors matters, not just performance on familiar materials or unworn sensors. The force-matched, deformation-only contacts are important negative cases because deformation must not be mistaken for impending slip simply because force conditions are comparable.
Can you unpack the difference between predicting slip and detecting deformation? Both might be visible in tactile contact.

They differ in what the prediction is meant to indicate. Impending grasp slip means a slip event is approaching; elastic deformation alone means the contact changes shape without that slip. The objective is not to ignore deformation altogether. It is to avoid treating deformation-only contact as evidence sufficient to announce slip. The node does not specify a particular tactile signature for either situation, so it would be premature to claim that any particular signal separates them.
So deformation-only contact is specifically a case where a slip warning could be wrong?

Yes. For this goal, a slip warning on a deformation-only contact would be a false alarm. Such contacts matter explicitly here, including ones matched for force. Matching force makes the comparison more demanding in that a warning cannot be justified merely by a difference in that matched quantity. It does not mean every other aspect of the contacts is identical.
What exactly does the 100-millisecond requirement ask for?

It asks for an advance prediction: the warning about impending grasp slip must arrive at least 100 milliseconds before the slip it concerns. Recognizing slip at the moment it occurs, or only afterward, would not satisfy that lead-time requirement. The goal does not specify a longer prediction window or a particular convention for marking the slip time, so neither should be assumed here.
If a warning came very close to slip but was usually right, would that meet the goal?

Not on that basis alone. The warning must meet the specified lead time as well as the stated recall and false-positive limits. Being accurate about a slip that is already occurring, or about to occur in less than 100 milliseconds, does not by itself establish the required advance prediction.
And the 90% recall refers to catching the impending slips?

Right. A recall of at least 90% means the predictor must identify at least 90% of the relevant slip cases under the required prediction condition. In this goal, that includes the advance-warning requirement rather than simply recognizing that slip happened eventually. The statement does not spell out a detailed counting protocol, but it does make clear that missed impending slips cannot exceed what that recall threshold allows.
How should I read the 5% false-positive rate alongside that?

It is a separate constraint on incorrect slip warnings for non-slip cases: the false-positive rate must be no more than 5%. Raising recall by warning on nearly every contact would not be enough if that also produced too many warnings during deformation-only contact. Both numerical targets have to be met while predicting at least 100 milliseconds ahead.
Does the false-positive requirement specifically matter for the force-matched deformation-only contacts?

Yes; they are explicitly included among the conditions the goal must handle. They test the distinction the objective calls for: an elastic change without grasp slip should not be mistaken for impending slip, even when the contact is matched for force. The statement does not provide a separate numerical false-positive threshold for that subset; the stated limit is ≤5%.
Why mention held-out materials rather than just materials in general?

Held-out materials make generalization an explicit part of the requirement. The prediction cannot be judged solely by whether it works on materials it has already encountered in the relevant development setting. The goal requires the timing, recall, and false-positive targets to be met on held-out materials as well. It does not identify particular materials or prescribe how they are selected.
Does sensor wear serve a similar purpose, or is it a different condition?

It is another explicit condition under which the same targets must hold. The objective says the predictor should distinguish impending slip from elastic deformation across sensor wear and should meet the numerical targets on worn sensors. It does not specify a degree of wear, a wear mechanism, or how wear is measured, so the requirement should be expressed without assuming any of those details.
Am I asking for good performance separately on held-out materials and on worn sensors?

The wording requires the targets on held-out materials and worn sensors; neither condition can be left out when describing success. It also calls out force-matched deformation-only contacts. It does not define the exact breakdown of test groups or state a particular aggregation rule, so I would preserve all those conditions without inventing a more detailed evaluation layout.
Could a predictor satisfy the goal by treating any noticeable elastic deformation as a slip precursor?

Not if that leads it to announce slip during deformation-only contacts, particularly the force-matched ones included in the requirement. The requested distinction is between an approaching grasp slip and elastic deformation that does not become slip. Nothing in the goal says deformation can never accompany slip; it says deformation by itself must not be conflated with an impending slip event.
What if it avoids false alarms by almost never predicting slip?

That would have to be checked against the ≥90% recall requirement. A predictor that rarely warns may keep false positives low but miss too many impending slips. Conversely, one that warns too freely might achieve high recall while breaching the ≤5% false-positive limit. The goal requires both, together with the ≥100-millisecond warning.
Is there a specified technique for reaching those numbers?

No technique is specified. The request sets a behavioral goal for tactile prediction and gives performance and generalization conditions. It does not name a model, sensor design, tactile feature, training procedure, or experimental result. Those details should not be presented as if they were already part of the goal.
I also don't want the description to sound as though the targets have already been achieved.

Agreed. This is a development objective, not a report of demonstrated performance. The precise statement is that tactile slip prediction should distinguish impending grasp slip from elastic deformation across unseen materials and sensor wear, with predictions at least 100 milliseconds early, ≥90% recall, and ≤5% false-positive rate. Those targets are to be met on held-out materials and worn sensors, including force-matched deformation-only contacts.
What is the central failure that the deformation-only examples are meant to reveal?

They reveal false slip warnings where the contact deforms elastically but does not slip. Because the stated examples are matched for force, they keep the comparison focused on distinguishing the outcomes rather than merely separating cases by the matched force. That is a description of the requirement, not a claim that any particular predictor has succeeded or failed on those examples.
Can I say the objective is robust anticipation rather than just classification?

Yes, if “robust” refers to the stated conditions rather than an unmeasured property. “Anticipation” captures the at-least-100-millisecond lead time, while the distinction from elastic deformation and the tests on held-out materials and worn sensors capture the requested generalization. The numerical meaning should remain explicit: ≥90% recall and ≤5% false-positive rate, including the force-matched deformation-only contacts.

For the tactile slip-prediction goal, I propose training a wear-invariant 100-ms slip-hazard model on viscoelastic-corrected tactile shear, contrasting it with force-matched deformation-only contacts.

That is a proposed approach, not a demonstrated result. It makes the prediction target a slip hazard at the 100-millisecond horizon, uses viscoelastic-corrected tactile shear as the model input, and explicitly contrasts impending slip with deformation-only contact under matched force. Calling the model wear-invariant states what the training is intended to achieve; it does not yet establish that its predictions remain reliable on worn sensors.
What does “slip hazard” convey here?

It conveys a prediction about approaching slip, rather than a label saying that slip is already occurring. The “100-ms” description ties that prediction to the advance-warning timescale in the goal. It does not, on its own, specify the model’s output format, a probability-calibration method, or a rule for issuing warnings.
Should I interpret 100 ms as predicting the exact instant of slip?

No. A 100-ms slip-hazard model is framed around anticipating slip on that timescale, not necessarily estimating an exact slip timestamp. The broader requirement remains a prediction at least 100 milliseconds ahead. The proposal does not provide a more detailed definition of the prediction window.
Why specify tactile shear instead of just saying tactile input?

Because the proposal names a particular kind of tactile information: shear. Keeping that term makes the proposed input more precise than the general phrase “tactile input.” It does not specify which sensor supplies it, how it is represented, or which other inputs, if any, might be considered.
And what does the viscoelastic correction add to that description?

It says the proposed shear input is viscoelastic-corrected, rather than unqualified tactile shear. Conceptually, the correction is relevant to the aim of separating an impending slip signal from changes associated with elastic deformation. But the proposal does not define the correction, identify a viscoelastic model, or establish how much that correction helps. Those would be additional details, not facts already supplied.
I don't want “corrected” to imply we've already removed every deformation effect.

It need not imply that. Here, “viscoelastic-corrected” describes the intended form of the shear used to train the model. It is not a claim that deformation effects have been completely eliminated, that the correction is perfect on unseen materials, or that the slip/deformation distinction has already been achieved.
What exactly is being contrasted with what?

The contrast is between the slip-hazard cases the model is meant to recognize and deformation-only contacts it should not mistake for impending slip. Those deformation-only contacts are matched for force. The wording does not specify a particular pairing procedure, contrastive objective, or number of examples; it specifies the important comparison.
Why does matching force matter to this proposal?

It keeps a simple force difference from standing in for the distinction the model is supposed to learn. The challenging comparison is a contact that deforms without slipping versus one associated with impending slip, under matched force. Force matching does not assert that the contacts are identical in every other respect or guarantee that the model will distinguish them.
Could the model still use the fact that deformation is present?

The proposal does not prohibit using information associated with deformation. Its point is that deformation alone should not be treated as equivalent to impending slip. Training against force-matched deformation-only contacts is intended to confront that ambiguity rather than assume that every changing tactile shear signal predicts slip.
How strong a claim is “wear-invariant” at this stage?

It is an intended property of the model to be trained. It expresses the aim that sensor wear should not determine whether the slip-hazard prediction works. The proposal does not identify a way of enforcing invariance, quantify permissible wear effects, or report performance on worn sensors, so it should not be phrased as a verified property.
Does wear-invariant mean identical outputs from every worn and unworn sensor?

That would be more specific than the proposal says. “Wear-invariant” signals a goal of robustness to sensor wear for the relevant slip prediction; it does not prescribe exact equality of outputs across sensors or wear conditions. The pertinent question remains whether the model can make the required distinction when sensors are worn.
How does this proposal relate to the held-out-material condition?

The proposal is directed at the same broader goal, which includes performance on held-out materials. Its use of viscoelastic-corrected tactile shear and force-matched deformation-only comparisons is a proposed route toward a transferable distinction, not evidence that transfer to held-out materials has occurred. Nothing here specifies particular materials or results on them.
If we train the model this way, can we say it meets the ≥90% recall and ≤5% false-positive-rate targets?

No. Those are performance requirements for the goal, whereas this node proposes a way to train a model. Training on viscoelastic-corrected tactile shear and contrasting force-matched deformation-only contacts does not itself establish ≥90% recall, ≤5% false-positive rate, or success at least 100 milliseconds before slip on held-out materials and worn sensors.
Could I describe the force-matched deformation-only contacts as negative examples without specifying anything else?

In the context of predicting slip hazard, yes: they are contacts for which an impending-slip warning would be inappropriate because they involve deformation only. That describes their role in the proposed contrast. It should not be expanded into an unstated sampling scheme, annotation procedure, or claim that all non-slip contacts look like them.
Would a slip-hazard model trained on the corrected shear automatically solve the deformation problem?

No automatic success follows from the named input or the hazard framing. The proposal brings the deformation-only comparison into training precisely because distinguishing deformation from approaching slip is the point at issue. Whether the trained model actually makes that distinction, especially under sensor wear and on held-out materials, remains to be shown.
Can you state the proposal in one sentence without making it sound like a completed experiment?

Propose training a wear-invariant 100-ms slip-hazard model using viscoelastic-corrected tactile shear, with force-matched deformation-only contacts as a contrasting condition for learning to distinguish impending grasp slip from elastic deformation.
Does that sentence commit us to any particular model architecture or correction algorithm?

No. It names the intended model property, prediction timescale, input description, and comparison condition, but leaves the architecture and the method for viscoelastic correction unspecified. Likewise, it states no training outcome.
The question I want to examine is: which viscoelastic-corrected shear features distinguish slip 100 ms ahead from force-matched elastic recoil under taxel wear?

That is an open feature-discrimination question. It asks which aspects of viscoelastic-corrected tactile shear, if any, provide advance evidence of slip rather than merely reflecting elastic recoil, when force is matched and taxels are worn. The question does not identify the distinguishing features or establish that the correction already makes the two cases separable.
What is the significance of saying “100 ms ahead” in the question?

It makes timing part of the distinction. A feature that becomes recognizable only when slip occurs would not answer which features distinguish it 100 milliseconds ahead. The question concerns what the corrected shear can indicate in advance, while elastic recoil remains a competing explanation for the tactile change.
So a feature could distinguish the two afterward and still not answer this?

Exactly. Retrospective differences are not necessarily predictive differences. The question asks specifically about discrimination 100 ms before slip, not about identifying slip after the fact or distinguishing the completed events.
How should I understand “force-matched elastic recoil” here?

It is the comparison case: elastic recoil without the impending slip of interest, under matched force. Matching force keeps the question from being answered simply by pointing to a force difference between the cases. It does not say that recoil and impending slip have identical corrected shear or are matched in every other respect.
Is elastic recoil just another name for slip in this question?

No. The question depends on keeping them distinct. It asks what in the corrected shear indicates slip is coming, as opposed to a force-matched elastic response that could otherwise be mistaken for such an indication.
Why include “viscoelastic-corrected” rather than asking about raw shear features?

Because the question is specifically about features of shear after viscoelastic correction. It does not ask whether raw shear has distinguishing features, nor does it say the correction perfectly removes recoil-related effects. Whether the corrected signal contains a useful distinction is precisely what remains open.
Does “features” imply we already know what representation to use?

No. Here, “features” names the aspects of the corrected shear that might carry the distinction; it does not specify a representation or list of candidates. Supplying a particular feature as the answer without further information would turn the question into an unsupported finding.
What does taxel wear add to the question?

It makes the sought distinction conditional on wear at the tactile sensing elements. The question is not merely whether corrected shear can distinguish impending slip from recoil in an unspecified sensor condition. It asks which distinguishing features remain relevant under taxel wear, without specifying the degree of wear or how it changes the measurements.
Would it be accurate to say taxel wear definitely changes the corrected shear in a particular way?

Not from this question alone. Taxel wear is an explicit condition to contend with, but no particular effect on corrected shear is stated. We can ask whether a putative feature still distinguishes the cases under wear; we cannot assert a specific wear-induced change as an established fact here.
Can I treat a feature that responds strongly to both impending slip and recoil as distinguishing them?

Not merely because it responds strongly. To answer the question, a feature would need to help tell the approaching-slip case apart from force-matched elastic recoil at the specified advance time, under taxel wear. A response shared by both could reflect their similarity rather than provide the needed distinction.
Does matching force settle the recoil ambiguity?

No. Force matching defines a demanding comparison; it does not settle its outcome. The open question is whether viscoelastic-corrected shear contains features that separate those cases despite that match and despite taxel wear.
How does this question connect to the proposed slip-hazard model?

The proposed model would use viscoelastic-corrected tactile shear to anticipate slip while contrasting deformation-only contacts. This question asks what discriminating information in that proposed input could support the distinction specifically 100 ms ahead, with force-matched elastic recoil as the comparison under taxel wear. It asks for the basis of a prediction rather than assuming that the proposed model has found one.
Would naming a feature here mean the broader recall and false-positive targets were met?

No. Even identifying a candidate distinction would not, by itself, demonstrate the broader performance targets. This node asks which corrected-shear features distinguish the cases at the stated lead time under taxel wear; it reports neither an identified feature nor a measured predictive result.
Can the question be expressed without presuming such a feature exists?

Yes: “Are there features of viscoelastic-corrected tactile shear that distinguish impending slip 100 ms ahead from force-matched elastic recoil under taxel wear, and if so, which ones?” That preserves the comparison and conditions while making the uncertainty explicit.

Here is a hypothesis for the feature question: spatially propagating shear-residual fronts emerge at least 100 milliseconds before slip, but not during force-matched elastic recoil, even on unseen materials and worn taxels.

That proposes a particular distinguishing feature: a front in the shear residual that propagates spatially before slip. The hypothesized contrast is its presence at least 100 milliseconds before slip and its absence in force-matched recoil. The claim is also meant to hold on unseen materials and with worn taxels. At this point, those are predictions of the hypothesis, not observed results.
What does “spatially propagating” add beyond saying that the shear residual changes?

It says the hypothesized change has a pattern that advances across space. A residual could change without forming a propagating front; the hypothesis singles out the front-like progression as the possible distinction. It does not specify a direction, speed, or exact shape for that progression.
And “shear residual” refers to the corrected shear we've been discussing?

Yes, that is the context for the term here: the proposed feature is in the shear residual associated with viscoelastic-corrected tactile shear. The hypothesis does not define a formula for the residual or claim that the correction removes every effect of elastic deformation.
Does the hypothesis say that no shear residual appears during recoil?

No. Its contrast concerns spatially propagating shear-residual fronts, not the existence of any residual at all. Force-matched recoil could have a changing residual without exhibiting the particular front described in the hypothesis. Whether that contrast actually occurs remains open.
How should I read “at least 100 milliseconds before slip”?

The hypothesized front would emerge no later than 100 milliseconds before the slip event it is meant to anticipate. A front appearing only at slip, afterward, or less than 100 milliseconds beforehand would not match that timing claim. The wording does not set an exact emergence time beyond the minimum lead time.
So a front first visible 100 ms before slip fits, and an earlier one could fit too?
Yes. The “≥100 ms before” condition includes emergence at the 100-millisecond lead time or earlier. It should not be paraphrased as emerging exactly 100 milliseconds before every slip.
Does the hypothesis imply the front is the cause of slip?

No. It proposes an advance distinguishing pattern in the shear residual. Temporal precedence and predictive relevance would not, by themselves, establish that the front causes slip. The hypothesis is about what might be visible before slip compared with force-matched recoil.
Why retain force matching in the recoil comparison?

Because the proposed distinction is supposed to survive a comparison in which force is matched. The hypothesis cannot be reduced to “the two cases have different forces.” It predicts a difference in the spatially propagating residual-front pattern between impending slip and elastic recoil under that matched condition.
Does it claim that elastic recoil never has a moving pattern of any kind?

No. The stated claim is narrower: the proposed spatially propagating shear-residual fronts emerge ahead of slip but not in force-matched recoil. It does not characterize every possible pattern in recoil or make a universal statement about all elastic contacts.
What work are “unseen materials” and “worn taxels” doing in the hypothesis?

They extend the proposed distinction beyond familiar material conditions and unworn tactile sensing elements. The hypothesis predicts that the advance front-versus-recoil contrast persists even on unseen materials and with worn taxels. It does not identify particular materials, amounts of wear, or a mechanism that would make the pattern persist.
Could I say we've found a wear-invariant feature now?

Not yet. You can say the hypothesis *proposes* a feature expected to distinguish the cases even with worn taxels. Calling it a found, wear-invariant feature would turn an untested claim into a result. The same caution applies to its proposed behavior on unseen materials.
Is the idea simply that slip produces a larger residual than recoil?

That is not what this hypothesis specifies. Its distinguishing claim concerns spatial propagation of a residual front and when it emerges, not a stated difference in residual magnitude. A magnitude comparison would be an additional claim.
Could a residual change at several taxels at once count as a propagating front?

The wording points to a front that advances spatially, rather than merely a change observed at multiple locations. It does not supply a formal criterion for deciding when a pattern qualifies as a front, so it would be better not to impose a particular rule here.
What if a similar front appears during force-matched recoil?

That would challenge the proposed distinction: the hypothesis specifically predicts that such fronts do not emerge in the force-matched recoil comparison. It would not be faithful to describe that outcome as consistent with the hypothesis merely because residual shear changed in both cases.
And if a front appears before slip but only shortly beforehand?

A front emerging less than 100 milliseconds before slip would not satisfy the hypothesis’s lead-time claim, even if it distinguished slip from recoil at that later moment. Both the spatial contrast and the ≥100-millisecond timing are part of the prediction.
Does this hypothesis answer the earlier question about which feature might distinguish the cases?

It offers a candidate answer: spatially propagating shear-residual fronts. But it remains a hypothesis about that feature’s timing and its absence in force-matched recoil under the stated material and wear conditions, not a settled identification of a distinguishing feature.
Would confirming this pattern automatically establish the full slip-prediction performance target?

No. A distinctive pattern emerging at least 100 milliseconds before slip would speak to the proposed feature and its timing. It would not, without further performance evidence, establish ≥90% recall and ≤5% false-positive rate on held-out materials and worn sensors, including force-matched deformation-only contacts.
Can you restate the hypothesis without implying that it has already been observed?

The hypothesis is that spatially propagating fronts in viscoelastic-corrected shear residuals emerge at least 100 milliseconds before grasp slip, but not during force-matched elastic recoil, and that this contrast persists on unseen materials and with worn taxels.
I want to run SlipRecoil-v1 leave-material-and-wear-out tests with force-matched recoil controls, and measure slip recall at least 100 milliseconds ahead and the deformation false-positive rate.

That describes a test activity, not a result. SlipRecoil-v1 names the tests; the leave-material-and-wear-out condition puts generalization across materials and sensor wear in view. The force-matched recoil controls address the competing explanation that a tactile change reflects elastic deformation rather than impending slip. The two specified measurements are recall for slip predictions made ≥100 ms ahead and the false-positive rate on deformation contacts.
What does the leave-material-and-wear-out condition contribute to this test?

It prevents the evaluation from being described solely in terms of familiar material and wear conditions. The intended question is whether the advance slip distinction holds when materials and wear conditions are left out of the relevant development setting. The activity does not specify the particular materials, wear states, or splitting procedure, so those should remain unspecified.
Does that wording mean we have already shown the method generalizes?
No. It describes the conditions under which to test generalization. It does not report what SlipRecoil-v1 found, or even that the tests have been completed.
Why include force-matched recoil controls rather than only examples of slip?

Recall on slip cases alone would not tell you how often elastic recoil produces an erroneous slip warning. Force-matched recoil controls provide the non-slip comparison relevant to that ambiguity. Their force matching means the proposed distinction cannot be credited merely to a difference in the matched force; it does not imply that the contacts are identical in every other respect.
Is a warning on one of those recoil controls what we're calling a deformation false positive?

Yes. In this activity, the recoil control is a deformation case rather than an impending-slip case. Treating it as an advance slip warning would be a deformation false positive. Measuring that rate complements measuring how often actual slip cases receive an early warning.
Why specify recall as “≥100-ms-ahead slip recall” instead of simply “slip recall”?

Because the lead time is essential. A warning that recognizes a slip only as it happens, or less than 100 milliseconds beforehand, should not be conflated with one that predicts it at least 100 milliseconds ahead. The requested recall measurement concerns the latter.
Does ≥100 ms mean exactly 100 ms before each slip?

No. It means at least 100 milliseconds before slip, so an earlier qualifying warning also fits the timing condition. The activity does not specify a narrower prediction window or a detailed counting convention.
And the deformation false-positive rate is separate from that recall measurement?

Yes. The recall measurement concerns advance warnings for slip cases; the deformation false-positive rate concerns erroneous warnings for deformation cases. Reporting one without the other would leave out part of the stated evaluation.
How does this activity bear on the hypothesis about spatially propagating shear-residual fronts?

It is intended to evaluate the hypothesized advance distinction between slip and force-matched recoil, including under material and wear variation. The specified measurements ask whether slip can be anticipated at least 100 ms ahead without frequent false warnings on deformation. The activity does not separately specify a measurement or scoring rule for the fronts themselves, so the outcomes of those two rates should not automatically be described as direct observations of a front.
If early recall is high, could I conclude that the proposed fronts occurred?

Not from that measurement alone. Early recall describes prediction performance, not which feature produced the warnings. The front hypothesis is the motivation for the evaluation, but this activity only explicitly names the tests, controls, and two performance measurements. A claim that fronts occurred would need support not stated here.
What if the deformation false-positive rate is low? Would that prove the front is absent during recoil?

A low false-positive rate would describe how rarely deformation cases triggered erroneous slip warnings. By itself, it would not prove that no spatially propagating shear-residual front appeared during recoil. Prediction behavior and direct characterization of the proposed feature are related questions, but they are not interchangeable.
Can I say the test includes worn taxels?

You can say it includes the stated wear-out evaluation condition and is relevant to the question under taxel wear. The activity does not give a particular taxel-wear level, define how wear is imposed or measured, or report results for worn taxels.
Should I specify which materials are held out when describing SlipRecoil-v1?

Not unless that information is supplied separately. The current activity identifies leave-material-and-wear-out tests but does not name the materials or give the composition of the held-out conditions. Inventing those details would make the description more specific than the plan.
Does the activity commit to a particular model architecture or a method for calculating the shear residual?

No. It calls for running SlipRecoil-v1 tests with the stated controls and measuring the two outcomes. It does not specify an architecture, a residual calculation, or a procedure for detecting a propagating front.
Could the tests be described as successful merely because they ran?

No. Running the tests is the activity; success on the slip-prediction objective would depend on the measurements, which have not been provided here. The wording should keep the planned evaluation distinct from any claim about its outcome.
Give me a concise description that preserves both metrics and the comparison.

Run SlipRecoil-v1 leave-material-and-wear-out tests using force-matched recoil controls, and measure ≥100-ms-ahead slip recall alongside the deformation false-positive rate. No test result is implied by that description.
I have the SlipRecoil-v1 result: on held-out materials and worn taxels, propagating fronts were observed, with 92% slip recall at 100 ms and 3.8% deformation false positives.

That reports three findings from SlipRecoil-v1: propagating fronts were observed under the stated held-out-material and worn-taxel conditions; slip recall was 92% at 100 milliseconds; and the deformation false-positive rate was 3.8%. The report gives those observations and measurements, but not a breakdown by material or wear condition.
When I say “propagating fronts,” which fronts are we talking about?

In this context, the spatially propagating shear-residual fronts discussed as a possible advance slip feature. The new result says they were observed on held-out materials and worn taxels. It does not specify their shape, direction, speed, or how individual fronts were identified.
Does the observation mean we can say those fronts caused the model's predictions?

No. Observing fronts alongside a recall measurement does not, by itself, establish that the fronts caused particular predictions. The result reports their presence and the measured prediction outcomes, without attributing each warning to that feature.
How precisely should the timing result be stated?

State it as 92% slip recall at 100 ms. That preserves the reported measurement. It would be more specific than this result to claim the same recall at every earlier lead time, or to give an exact time at which each observed front first emerged.
Is the 3.8% figure the rate of deformation contacts incorrectly flagged as slip?

Yes. Here, “3.8% deformation false positives” reports the false-positive rate for deformation cases: erroneous slip warnings on contacts that were deformation cases. The SlipRecoil-v1 evaluation included force-matched recoil controls, but this result does not provide a separate false-positive figure for that control subset.
Can I infer that propagating fronts never occurred in the force-matched recoil controls?

Not from this result as stated. It reports that propagating fronts were observed on held-out materials and worn taxels, together with slip recall and deformation false positives. It does not give a direct count or explicit observation of fronts in the force-matched recoil controls. A deformation false-positive rate is not the same thing as a measurement of whether a front appeared there.
Does “held-out materials and worn taxels” tell us the separate recall for each condition?

No. Those are the conditions named for the SlipRecoil-v1 result, but the statement supplies one recall figure, 92% at 100 ms, and one deformation false-positive figure, 3.8%. It does not report separate values for individual held-out materials, particular worn taxels, or each condition considered on its own.
Could I describe the fronts as appearing at least 100 ms before every slip?

That would go beyond the reported evidence. The 100-ms figure is attached to the slip-recall measurement. The result says propagating fronts were observed, but does not give a front-emergence time for every slip or say that a front appeared in every slip case.
What is the safest way to connect the front observation to the two percentages?

Present them as findings from the same SlipRecoil-v1 result without claiming a stronger link than was reported: propagating fronts were observed on held-out materials and worn taxels; slip recall was 92% at 100 ms; and deformation false positives were 3.8%. That leaves open exactly how the observed fronts relate to individual correct or incorrect predictions.
Should I call 3.8% a false-positive rate rather than a count?
Yes. A percentage of deformation false positives is being reported as a rate, not as the number of false-positive contacts. The result does not state the number of deformation contacts tested.
Likewise, does 92% give the number of slip cases?
No. It gives slip recall at the specified 100-ms lead time. Without the number of slip cases, it cannot be turned into a count of correctly anticipated slips.
Can you give me a compact result statement that doesn't add those missing details?
On SlipRecoil-v1, propagating shear-residual fronts were observed on held-out materials and worn taxels, with 92% slip recall at 100 ms and a 3.8% deformation false-positive rate.
I’m selecting propagating shear-residual fronts as the primary cue for slip prediction. The reason is that held-out 100-ms slip recall reached 92%, with 3.8% deformation false positives.

That is a decision to prioritize propagating shear-residual fronts as the cue, grounded in the stated held-out measurements: 92% slip recall at 100 ms and a 3.8% deformation false-positive rate. “Primary” indicates the leading cue for this decision; it does not say that no other information may be used.
What is the distinction between calling the fronts the primary cue and calling them the only cue?

“Primary” gives them priority in the prediction approach. “Only” would exclude every other possible cue, which the decision does not do. The statement selects what to emphasize without specifying a complete set of permitted or excluded inputs.
Does the decision claim that every correctly anticipated slip had a front?

No. The 92% figure is a held-out slip-recall measurement at 100 ms, not a case-by-case account of which cue appeared for each correct prediction. Selecting fronts as the primary cue should not be turned into a claim that they occurred in every correctly anticipated slip.
Is 92% describing how often a front appeared, then?

Not as stated. It describes slip recall at the 100-ms lead time. The decision connects that measured predictive performance to the choice of a primary cue, but it does not give a separate percentage for the occurrence of fronts.
Why include the deformation figure in the reason for selecting the cue?

Because advance slip prediction also has to avoid mistaking deformation for slip. The cited 3.8% deformation false-positive rate addresses that side of the distinction. I’d like to propose another approach to the tactile slip-prediction goal: train a physics-guided state-space model that separates reversible strain from irreversible interfacial creep, using force-matched negatives and wear augmentation.

It offers a way to frame the ambiguity between a contact that deforms and can recover and an interfacial change that does not simply reverse. It names a persistent change associated with the contact interface, in contrast to reversible strain. That is the distinction the proposed state-space model is intended to represent. The proposal does not give a measurement rule for creep, define how irreversible it must be, or say that every instance of creep culminates in grasp slip.

Right. The proposal separates types of contact behavior to support prediction; it does not define interfacial creep as a completed slip. Nor does it state that identifying creep would automatically provide a warning at the required lead time.

It says physical considerations should guide the model’s treatment of reversible strain and irreversible interfacial creep. Not from this proposal alone. It proposes training a model to separate creep from reversible strain; it does not specify a direct creep measurement or establish that the model’s eventual representation corresponds uniquely to measured physical creep.

ShearFront-v2 is retained there. The decision does not assign that region to the revived gated dither. The decision names where each approach is to be used, while the numbers retain the scope of the evaluations from which they came. Keeping those distinct avoids claiming that every future contact in either region will reproduce its cited percentages.

No. FPR concerns erroneous slip warnings on recoil contacts, not missed slip cases. Recall concerns correct advance predictions on slip cases. The two measures have different denominators.
Is 100 ms also the timing rule for those recoil false positives?
The 100-ms qualifier belongs to slip recall. Neither cited recoil FPR is specified here as a rate calculated at an exact point 100 ms before a recoil event, so that timing rule should not be added.
